title: Switching mid-action
plainEnglish: It says you were doing one action and then, partway through, switched to or were interrupted by another.
whenToUse: Use it when you stop one action partway and move to a second one, often unexpectedly. Example: 집에 가다가 편의점에 들렀어요 (I was on my way home and stopped by the convenience store).
attachmentRule: Attach -다가 (often shortened to -다) straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (가다→가다가, 먹다→먹다가, 보다→보다가). The subject of both clauses must be the same person, and the first action is left unfinished. For a finished action that then leads to a result, you can use the past stem -았/었다가 (갔다가 = went and then came back).
contrastWith: -다가 means you cut one action short to do another, while -고 나서 means you fully finish the first action before starting the second.

examples.en: I was on my way home and ran into a friend.
I was watching a drama and fell asleep.
I was working and suddenly got a headache.
I was riding the bus and got motion sick.

commonMistakes: Using -다가 with two different subjects; both actions must be done by the same person.
Conjugating the verb before -다가, like 먹어다가; attach it to the plain stem, so 먹다가.

practiceItems.prompt: I was going home and (met a friend)
I was watching a drama and (fell asleep)
I was working and (suddenly got a headache)

studyOrder: Find the first action you start but do not finish
Attach -다가 to its plain stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
Add the new or interrupting action in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: V-다가 captures that very common moment when you are in the middle of doing something and then switch to, or get interrupted by, something else. You simply glue -다가 (you will often hear it cut to just -다) onto the plain verb stem, so 가다 becomes 가다가 and 보다 becomes 보다가. A picture helps: 집에 가다가 친구를 만났어요 means I was heading home and ran into a friend along the way, with the first action left hanging. Two rules keep it natural: the same person must do both actions, and you attach it to the bare stem, never a conjugated form like 먹어다가. Compare it with -고 나서, where you completely finish the first action before moving on, whereas -다가 cuts the first action short.

title: Because of (sudden, bad) cause
plainEnglish: It gives a sudden or unintended reason that caused an unwanted result.
whenToUse: Use it to blame an unexpected action or event for a negative outcome. Example: 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지하철을 놓쳤어요 (I overslept, so I missed the subway).
attachmentRule: Attach -는 바람에 to a verb stem (자다→자는 바람에, 막히다→막히는 바람에). It only goes on action verbs, not adjectives, and even though it describes a past result you keep the form as -는 바람에, not a past form. The result clause is almost always negative or unplanned and is normally in the past tense.
contrastWith: -는 바람에 blames a sudden, usually bad and unintended cause, while -아/어서 is a neutral all-purpose because that works for good or bad results alike.

examples.en: I overslept, so I was late to work.
The traffic was jammed, so I was late to my appointment.

examples.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
examples.en: It suddenly rained, so I got soaked.
The person next to me shoved me, so I fell over.

commonMistakes: Attaching it to an adjective, like 바쁜 바람에; it goes only on action verbs.
Putting it on a past stem, like 잤는 바람에; keep it as the present -는 바람에 even when the result is past.

practiceItems.prompt: I overslept, so (I was late to work)
the traffic was jammed, so (I was late)
it suddenly rained, so (I got soaked)
practiceItems.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
practiceItems.answer: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.

studyOrder: Find the sudden action or event that caused trouble
Attach -는 바람에 to its verb stem
Keep it in the -는 form even for a past result
State the negative or unplanned result in the past tense
beginnerExplanation: V-는 바람에 is the connector you reach for when something unexpected goes wrong and you want to pin the blame on its cause. You add -는 바람에 to an action verb stem, so 자다 becomes 자는 바람에 and 막히다 becomes 막히는 바람에. The feel is always a sudden, usually unwanted cause leading to a bad result, as in 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지각했어요 (I overslept, so I was late). Two things trip learners up: it only attaches to action verbs, not adjectives, so 바쁜 바람에 is wrong; and even though the result already happened, you keep the present shape 자는 바람에, not 잤는 바람에. Think of it as a more dramatic, blame-assigning cousin of the plain because connector 아/어서.

title: I noticed X, then Y
plainEnglish: It links something you personally observed earlier to a result or change that followed.
whenToUse: Use it to report that you watched someone do or be something, and then a related outcome happened. Example: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 (My brother kept eating late-night snacks, and then he gained weight).
attachmentRule: Attach -더니 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (먹다→먹더니, 춥다→춥더니). For the typical use, the first clause is something you observed about another person or the weather, and the second clause is its natural result. With your own actions, the related form -았/었더니 (먹었더니) is used to mean after I did X, then Y happened.
contrastWith: -더니 reports a result you observed following someone else's past action, while -아/어서 simply gives a neutral cause without that sense of personal observation and contrast.

examples.ko: 동생이 매일 게임만 하더니 시험을 망쳤어요.
examples.en: My brother did nothing but game every day, and then he bombed the exam.
The weather was cold earlier, but now it is warm.

examples.ko: 친구가 한국어를 열심히 배우더니 이제 정말 잘해요.
examples.en: My friend studied Korean hard, and now she is really good at it.
The sky got cloudy, and then it started to rain.

commonMistakes: Using -더니 about your own present feelings; for plain first-person statements it sounds off, and -았/었더니 fits self-actions better.
Adding vowel harmony before -더니, like 먹어더니; attach it straight to the stem, so 먹더니.

practiceItems.prompt: he only gamed every day, and then (he bombed the exam)
it was cold earlier, but now (it is warm)
the sky got cloudy, and then (it started to rain)

studyOrder: Recall something you personally observed earlier
Attach -더니 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause the result or change that followed
For your own actions, switch to -았/었더니 instead
beginnerExplanation: V/A-더니 is how Korean ties together something you watched happen and the result or change that came after it, with a built-in sense of I saw this myself. You attach -더니 to the plain stem, so 먹다 becomes 먹더니 and 춥다 becomes 춥더니. It shines when describing other people or the weather: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 means my brother kept eating late-night snacks, and sure enough he gained weight. It can also mark a contrast over time, as in 아까는 춥더니 지금은 따뜻해요 (it was cold earlier, but now it is warm). The catch for beginners is the person: -더니 fits things you observed about others, while for your own actions you switch to -았/었더니, as in 운동했더니 다리가 아파요 (I worked out, and now my legs hurt).

title: Since I noticed, so I…
plainEnglish: It gives the reason you noticed that made you spontaneously do something yourself.
whenToUse: Use it when something you saw or heard prompted you to take an action on the spot. Example: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 (The strawberries were cheap, so I bought some).
attachmentRule: Attach -길래 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (싸다→싸길래, 울다→울길래, 먹다→먹길래). The first clause is the reason you perceived, and the second clause must be your own action and is usually in the past. For a noun reason use N(이)길래.
contrastWith: -길래 is a spoken, reason-based because that leads to your own spontaneous reaction, while -으니까 is a broader because that can also justify commands and suggestions, which -길래 cannot.

examples.en: The strawberries were cheap, so I bought two packs.
The child was crying, so I picked her up.
The weather was nice, so I came out for a walk.
My friend said it was delicious, so I ordered it too.

commonMistakes: Using a command or suggestion in the second clause, like ...길래 사세요; the result must be your own action, not an order to someone else.
Putting your own planned action as the reason; the first clause should be something you observed, not your own decision.

practiceItems.prompt: the strawberries were cheap, so (I bought two packs)
the child was crying, so (I picked her up)
the weather was nice, so (I came out for a walk)

studyOrder: Find what you saw or heard that prompted you
Attach -길래 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause your own reaction
Usually put your reaction in the past tense
beginnerExplanation: V/A-길래 is a friendly, spoken connector that explains the reason you noticed which pushed you to do something yourself, on the spot. You add -길래 straight to the stem, so 싸다 becomes 싸길래 and 울다 becomes 울길래. The classic shape is observation then my reaction: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 means the strawberries looked cheap, so I went ahead and bought some. The key restriction is that the second clause has to be your own action, very often in the past tense, so you cannot end with a command like 사세요. Think of it as warmer and more conversational than 으니까, and remember that 으니까 can justify suggestions and orders while 길래 only explains what made you, the speaker, act.

title: The more, the more
plainEnglish: It says as one thing increases, another thing changes along with it.
whenToUse: Use it for the more X, the more Y patterns. Example: 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets).
attachmentRule: Add -을수록 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹다→먹을수록, 작다→작을수록) and -ㄹ수록 to a stem ending in a vowel (가다→갈수록, 크다→클수록). ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ and take -ㄹ수록 (살다→살수록, 멀다→멀수록). It is very often paired with -(으)면 in front for emphasis, as in 보면 볼수록.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ수록 means the more of one thing brings more of another, a sliding scale, while -(으)니까 simply states a cause and effect without that increasing-together feeling.

examples.en: The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets.
The more I listen to this song, the more I like it.
The more people there are, the louder it gets.
The more I read this book, the harder it gets.

commonMistakes: Using -을수록 after a vowel stem, like 갈을수록; vowel stems take -ㄹ수록, so 갈수록.
Spacing it wrong as -ㄹ 수록; write 수록 attached, as in 할수록, not 할 수록.

practiceItems.prompt: the more I study Korean, (the more fun it gets)
the more I listen to this song, (the more I like it)
the more people there are, (the louder it gets)

studyOrder: Find the thing that increases
Add -을수록 after a consonant or -ㄹ수록 after a vowel
Optionally add -(으)면 in front for emphasis
Put the matching change in the second clause, often with 더
beginnerExplanation: V/A-(으)ㄹ수록 is the Korean version of the more, the more, describing how two things rise or change together on a sliding scale. The attachment follows the usual sound split: consonant stems take -을수록 (먹을수록, 작을수록) and vowel stems take -ㄹ수록 (갈수록, 클수록), while ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ first (살수록). A natural example is 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (the more you study Korean, the more fun it becomes), and Koreans love to double it up with -(으)면, as in 보면 볼수록 (the more you look). Two pitfalls: do not use -을수록 after a vowel, so it is 갈수록 not 갈을수록; and write 수록 right onto the verb, never spaced as 할 수록. Adding 더 (more) in the second clause makes the rising effect even clearer.

title: In order to
plainEnglish: It states the purpose or goal you are doing the main action for.
whenToUse: Use it for in order to do something, especially deliberate goals. Example: 살을 빼기 위해서 매일 운동해요 (I exercise every day in order to lose weight).
attachmentRule: Attach -기 위해서 (or the slightly more formal -기 위하여) to the plain verb stem with no change (빼다→빼기 위해서, 사다→사기 위해서). 위해 and 위해서 are interchangeable. For a noun goal, use N을/를 위해서 instead (가족을 위해서 = for my family). The subject usually intends the goal on purpose.
contrastWith: -기 위해서 expresses a deliberate purpose with an action verb goal, while -(으)러 also means in order to but only attaches to motion plans with 가다/오다, whereas 위해서 works with almost any main verb.

examples.en: I exercise every day in order to lose weight.

examples.ko: 한국 회사에 취직하기 위해서 한국어를 배워요.
examples.en: I am learning Korean in order to get a job at a Korean company.
I cut back on eating out in order to save money.
I quit smoking for the sake of my health.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 위해서, like 빼서 위해서; use the plain stem plus -기, so 빼기 위해서.
Using -기 위해서 with a noun; for nouns drop -기 and say N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서, not 가족기 위해서.

practiceItems.prompt: in order to lose weight (I exercise every day)
in order to save money (I cut back on eating out)
for the sake of my health (I quit smoking)

studyOrder: Decide the goal or purpose you are aiming for
If it is an action, add -기 위해서 to that verb stem
If it is a noun, use N을/를 위해서 instead
Put the action you take toward that goal in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-기 위해(서) is the clear, slightly formal way to state the purpose behind what you do, matching English in order to. For an action goal you add -기 위해서 to the plain stem, so 빼다 becomes 빼기 위해서 in 살을 빼기 위해서 운동해요 (I exercise in order to lose weight); 위해 and 위해서 mean the same thing. When the goal is a noun, you switch to N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서 (for my family), so do not jam 기 onto a noun. The most common slip is conjugating the verb first, like 빼서 위해서; always keep the bare stem plus 기. Compare it with -(으)러, which also means in order to but only pairs with going and coming verbs, while 기 위해서 works with nearly any main verb and stresses a deliberate goal.

title: Because / and then
plainEnglish: It links a cause to its result, or one action to the next closely connected one.
whenToUse: Use it to give a reason, or to show one action leading right into another with the same subject. Example: 늦어서 택시를 탔어요 (I was late, so I took a taxi).
attachmentRule: Build the 아/어 connective by vowel harmony: if the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use -아서 (가다→가서, 좋다→좋아서), otherwise use -어서 (먹다→먹어서, 늦다→늦어서); 하다 becomes 해서. Crucially, the first clause never takes a tense marker, so you say 늦어서, never 늦었어서, and you cannot use a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서.
contrastWith: -아/어서 gives a tight cause-result where the first clause stays tenseless and cannot lead to a command, while -(으)니까 is a because that allows commands and suggestions and can carry tense.

examples.en: I was hungry, so I made ramyeon.
The road was slippery, so I walked carefully.
I met my friend and we had coffee together.
I caught a cold, so I could not go to work.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 늦었어서; keep it tenseless as 늦어서 and mark tense only at the end.
Using a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서, like 피곤해서 쉬세요; for that use -(으)니까 instead.

practiceItems.prompt: I was hungry, so (I made ramyeon)
the road was slippery, so (I walked carefully)
I caught a cold, so (I could not go to work)

studyOrder: Find the cause or the first action
Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Keep that first clause tenseless
Add the result or next action, marking tense only at the end
beginnerExplanation: V/A-아/어서 is one of the most useful connectors in Korean, covering both because and a smooth and then between two linked actions. You form it with the same vowel harmony as the present tense: ㅏ or ㅗ stems take -아서 (가서, 좋아서), other stems take -어서 (먹어서, 늦어서), and 하다 becomes 해서. So 배가 고파서 라면을 끓였어요 means I was hungry, so I made ramyeon. Two rules are essential. First, the 아/어서 clause stays tenseless; you mark past or future only on the final verb, so it is 늦어서, never 늦었어서. Second, you cannot follow a reason 아/어서 with a command or suggestion, so for telling someone to rest because they are tired you must switch to 피곤하니까 쉬세요 using 으니까 instead.

title: As soon as
plainEnglish: It says the second action happens immediately after the first one finishes.
whenToUse: Use it for as soon as one thing happens, another follows right away. Example: 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (As soon as I got home, I lay down on the bed).
attachmentRule: Attach -자마자 straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change and regardless of consonant or vowel ending (오다→오자마자, 끝나다→끝나자마자, 받다→받자마자). It goes only on action verbs. The first clause carries no tense marker; the tense is shown on the final verb.
contrastWith: -자마자 stresses an immediate, back-to-back sequence with almost no gap, while -고 나서 means after finishing, allowing a normal gap of time between the two actions.

examples.en: As soon as I got home, I washed my hands.
As soon as the alarm rang, I got up.
As soon as class ended, I went straight home.
As soon as I got my paycheck, I spent it all.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 왔자마자; attach -자마자 to the plain stem, so 오자마자.
Using it for actions with a long gap between them; for that meaning use -고 나서, not -자마자.

practiceItems.prompt: as soon as I got home (I washed my hands)
as soon as the alarm rang (I got up)
as soon as class ended (I went straight home)

studyOrder: Find the first action that triggers the next
Attach -자마자 to its plain stem
Keep the first clause tenseless
Put the immediate next action in the second clause, often with 바로
beginnerExplanation: V-자마자 expresses that the moment one action finishes, the next one happens, just like English as soon as. It is wonderfully simple to attach: add -자마자 to the plain verb stem with no changes for vowels or consonants, so 오다 becomes 오자마자 and 받다 becomes 받자마자. A natural example is 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (the second I got home, I flopped onto the bed). Keep the first clause tenseless and mark tense only at the end, so write 오자마자, not 왔자마자. The nuance is immediacy with essentially no gap, which is why you often add 바로 (right away); when there is a normal pause between the two actions, use -고 나서 instead to mean simply after finishing.

title: So that / until
plainEnglish: It sets a goal or limit that the main action aims toward, often so that something happens.
whenToUse: Use it to do an action so that a result is reached, or to do something up to a point. Example: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 (I dress warmly so that I don't catch a cold).
attachmentRule: Attach -도록 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (늦다→늦도록, 알다→알도록, 들리다→들리도록). It commonly appears in the negative as -지 않도록 (so that ... not) and in advice or instructions. It can also mean until a point, as in 밤늦도록 (until late at night).
contrastWith: -도록 sets an aim or limit so that something is achieved, while -기 위해서 states a deliberate purpose; -도록 often points at a result or standard to keep, including not letting something happen.

examples.ko: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so that others can hear well.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.
examples.en: Dress warmly so that you do not catch a cold.
I made a note so that I would not forget.
I worked until late last night.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before -도록, like 듣어도록; attach it to the plain stem, so 듣도록.
Forgetting the natural negative shape -지 않도록 for so that ... not, like saying 안 늦도록 instead of 늦지 않도록.

practiceItems.prompt: so that others can hear well (please speak loudly)
practiceItems.ko: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.
practiceItems.answer: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.

practiceItems.prompt: so that you do not catch a cold (dress warmly)
practiceItems.ko: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.
practiceItems.answer: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.

practiceItems.prompt: so that I would not forget (I made a note)

studyOrder: Decide the result or limit you are aiming for
Attach -도록 to the verb stem
Use -지 않도록 when the goal is to prevent something
Put the action that works toward it in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-도록 marks the goal, standard, or limit that your main action is reaching toward, and it is everywhere in advice and instructions. You attach -도록 to the plain verb stem, so 듣다 becomes 듣도록 and 늦다 becomes 늦도록. Often the aim is to prevent something, which shows up as the negative -지 않도록: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 means I dress warmly so that I do not catch a cold. It can also mark a time limit meaning until, as in 밤늦도록 일했어요 (I worked until late at night). Two tips: attach it to the bare stem, not a harmonized form like 듣어도록; and for so that not, prefer the smooth 지 않도록 over patching 안 in front. It overlaps with 기 위해서 but leans toward a result or rule you want to keep.

title: Busy doing, so couldn't
plainEnglish: It gives a time- or effort-consuming action as the reason you could not do something else.
whenToUse: Use it when being busy with one action caused a negative result, like not finishing or being unable to do another. Example: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 (I was busy watching a drama, so I couldn't do my homework).
attachmentRule: Attach -느라(고) to an action verb stem with no vowel change (보다→보느라고, 일하다→일하느라고, 자다→자느라고); -느라 and -느라고 are interchangeable. The same person must do both actions, it goes only on action verbs, and the second clause is normally negative or apologetic. Do not add a tense marker before it.
contrastWith: -느라(고) blames a time- or effort-consuming action for a negative result with the same subject, while -아/어서 is a neutral because that allows positive results and different subjects too.

examples.en: I was busy gaming, so I missed your call.
I was busy with my part-time job, so I had no time to study.
I was busy looking after the kid, so I could not sleep a wink.
I was busy waiting for the bus, so I was late.

commonMistakes: Using it with an adjective or with two different subjects; it needs the same person doing an action verb.
Pairing it with a positive, happy result; the second clause should be a negative or unable outcome, so avoid things like 보느라고 행복했어요.

practiceItems.prompt: I was busy gaming, so (I missed your call)
I was busy with my part-time job, so (I had no time to study)
I was busy waiting for the bus, so (I was late)

studyOrder: Find the action that ate up your time or energy
Attach -느라(고) to that action verb stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
State the negative result, often with 못 or 안, in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: V-느라(고) explains that you were tied up doing one thing, and that is why something else did not get done. You attach -느라고 (or just -느라) to an action verb stem, so 보다 becomes 보느라고 and 일하다 becomes 일하느라고. The feel is always an excuse for a negative outcome with one subject: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 means I was busy watching a drama, so I could not do my homework. Three things keep it correct: it attaches only to action verbs, both actions must be done by the same person, and the result clause should be negative or apologetic, frequently with 못 or 안. That negative-result requirement is what separates it from the all-purpose 아/어서, which happily allows good results and different subjects.

title: After finishing
plainEnglish: It says you completely finish one action before starting the next.
whenToUse: Use it to stress that the first action is fully done, then you move on. Example: 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat).
attachmentRule: Attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change for both vowel and consonant endings (먹다→먹고 나서, 씻다→씻고 나서, 하다→하고 나서). It goes on action verbs only, since it implies completion. The tense is marked on the final verb, not on the -고 나서 clause.
contrastWith: -고 나서 highlights that the first action is fully completed before the next, while plain -고 just lists or sequences actions without stressing completion, and -다가 means you stopped the first action partway.

examples.en: I worked out and then took a shower.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.
examples.en: I have to take the medicine after eating.

examples.ko: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.
examples.en: I finished all my homework and then played games.

examples.ko: 이 영화를 보고 나서 책도 읽고 싶어요.
examples.en: After watching this movie, I want to read the book too.

commonMistakes: Using -고 나서 with an adjective; it needs an action verb because it implies finishing.
Adding tense before it, like 먹었고 나서; attach it to the plain stem and mark tense on the final verb.

after eating (I have to take medicine)
practiceItems.ko: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.
practiceItems.answer: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.

practiceItems.ko: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.
practiceItems.answer: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.

studyOrder: Find the action you fully complete first
Attach -고 나서 to its plain stem
Keep that clause tenseless
Put the next action in the second clause, marking tense at the end
beginnerExplanation: V-고 나서 tells the listener that you completely finish one action and only then start the next, putting a clear emphasis on completion. You attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no changes, so 먹다 becomes 먹고 나서 and 씻다 becomes 씻고 나서, as in 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat). Because it implies finishing, it only works with action verbs, and you mark tense on the final verb, never as 먹었고 나서. It is worth comparing three similar tools: plain -고 simply lists actions in order, -고 나서 stresses that the first one is done, and -다가 means you broke off the first action partway to do the second. When the finish really matters, 고 나서 is the natural choice.
